Working paper review · draft for discussion with Duncan

The Economics of Going Electric in California, Gas to Grid

NEM 3.0 hasn’t broken the economic case for home electrification. But it hasn’t delivered the battery-storage incentive it may have been designed to create.

commit c459506 branch main 260 tests passing 47 of 58 CA counties modeled
Claim 1 · Storage Claim 2 · Electrification vs. gas Claim 3 · Co-optimization value Limitations
CLAIM 1

Batteries don’t pencil out under NEM 3.0 at today’s prices. But PV and storage are economic complements

The co-optimization model chooses zero battery capacity at every real-world price point tested, in every county and utility territory checked. Optimal PV size shrinks in lockstep as battery cost rises. Without affordable storage, NEM 3.0’s low export credit makes larger solar systems uneconomic too.

$500–700per kWh. The threshold where battery starts to enter the optimal solution
~50–65%cost reduction needed from current real-world battery prices
0 kWhoptimal battery at NREL ATB 2025 pricing, in all 4 counties tested
On the discount-rate boundary: the sensitivity only becomes visible in non-PG&E territory. One reading: SCE and SDG&E’s rate structures reward battery dispatch enough that a low enough cost of capital tips the LP toward building some, while PG&E’s NEM 3.0 export economics don’t, at any rate tested. Worth a sentence in the paper as a boundary condition, not a caveat on the headline claim: at any discount rate a real household or utility program would use (typically 5-10% real), the battery conclusion is unchanged.

Tests backing this claim

  • TestLPSizingPriceMatchesReportingPrice (3 tests, lp_cooptimize_test.py). Proves the optimizer sizes PV and battery against the same $/kW and $/kWh price the report shows, not a stale hardcoded one.
  • TestBatteryStorageCost and TestSolarPanelCost (capital_costs_test.py). The two prices themselves match their cited sources (NREL ATB, CPUC), not a made-up number.
  • TestCapexMatchesEvaluationsPrimitives (lp_cooptimize_test.py). The annualization math (CRF, NPV) inside the LP matches the standalone formula used everywhere else in the pipeline.
  • TestLPBatteryRespondsToPriceSignal (3 tests, lp_cooptimize_test.py). Battery dispatch responds the way basic economics predicts, a check that the LP isn’t just returning zero by construction.
  • test_solar_storage_module_sizes_against_net_cost_for_the_configured_incentive_scenario (config_plumbing_test.py). Confirms the discount rate and incentive scenario used for the sensitivity sweep above actually reach the LP.

Sources

  • Battery cost. NREL Annual Technology Baseline 2025, residential storage, moderate scenario, via CEC report CEC-200-2024-011. $18,258 installed for a 5 kW / 12.5 kWh system.
  • Solar cost. CPUC-adopted 2023 California installed cost, $3.30/W, reconciling NREL ATB ($2.34/W) against LBNL Tracking the Sun ($3.80/W).
  • Discount rate. 7% real. See evaluations/constants.py. Sensitivity to this assumption is verified directly above, not just asserted.
CLAIM 2

Full electrification with properly-sized solar beats staying on gas. It wins in 46 of 47 California counties

Statewide median savings: 14.7% annualized cost, relative to staying on gas with solar. The one exception is Alpine County, because it has the highest heat-pump installation cost of any county in the dataset.

Tests backing this claim

  • TestHeatPumpSpaceCost and TestHeatPumpWaterHeaterCost (4 tests, capital_costs_test.py). Every one of the 47 pipeline counties’ heat pump costs is in a plausible range, and a missing county falls back to a computed median rather than a silent guess.
  • TestCARBAppliancesCost (4 tests, capital_costs_test.py). Induction stove and gas appliance costs match the underlying CARB data.
  • TestGasVsElectricCostOrdering (3 tests, capital_costs_test.py). Electric appliances cost more upfront than their gas equivalent in every county, the direction a reviewer would sanity-check first.
  • nem3_billing_test.py (24 tests). The NEM 3.0 billing math itself: export credit rates, fixed charges, carry-forward, cross-checked against the utility’s own published bill examples for 10 rate-plan and utility combinations.
  • energy_consumption_ballpark_test.py (30 tests). The underlying energy-use assumptions are benchmarked against EIA RECS, CEC RASS, and NREL ResStock survey data, not invented load shapes.
  • test_composite_key_preserves_other_scenarios_for_same_county (merge_and_write_csv_test.py). The exact bug class that caused an earlier data-loss incident, one county’s row silently overwriting another’s, can’t happen in the ledger these numbers come from.

Sources

  • Heat pump space heating & water heating. TECH Clean California program data (CEC), per-county contractor/turnkey cost, ducted systems only for space heating.
  • Induction stove, gas appliances. CARB appliance comparison data, 2022 costs inflated 3.4% CPI-U to 2023.
  • EV / ICE vehicle costs. DOE incremental purchase-cost methodology (2022); ICCT maintenance & insurance data.
  • Solar and battery sources as in Claim 1.
On the Alpine County exception: Alpine has the highest heat-pump space-heating cost of any county in the underlying TECH Clean California data ($24,962 vs. a statewide median of ~$19,400). This is consistent with a small, cold, high-elevation Sierra county. The co-optimizer correctly responds by building less system than the naive fixed-PV approach, but even the economically optimal system still costs slightly more than staying on gas there. Worth one sentence in the paper, not a caveat on the headline claim.
CLAIM 3

Sizing solar for the electrified load, not a rule of thumb, is worth real money, with zero exceptions

Co-optimizing PV size for the fully-electrified home, rather than using a fixed sizing heuristic, saves money in every one of 47 counties tested, with no exceptions. It’s the cleanest finding in this analysis.

$650mean annual savings from co-optimized vs. fixed PV sizing
$271–$826full range across all 47 counties
47 / 47counties where co-optimization wins. No exceptions

Distribution of co-optimization savings. A histogram or box plot of the $271–$826/yr savings across all 47 counties would make this the tightest, most visual claim in the paper. Every county lands on the same side of zero.

In the meantime, see Claim 2’s four county figures above: in each, the gap between the second bar (fixed-PV electrification) and third bar (co-optimized electrification) is this claim.

Tests backing this claim

  • co_optimization_test.py (3 tests). The co-optimizer’s reported capacities and cost components reconcile with each other, so a mis-wired reporting layer can’t quietly show one number while computing another.
  • solar_storage_dispatch_test.py (6 tests). The hour-by-hour dispatch physics (load balance, battery state-of-charge bounds, no double-counted energy) hold at every timestep, for every county.
  • step23_compare_coopt_vs_fixed_dispatch_test.py. The specific fixed-vs-co-optimized comparison this claim rests on reads the right cost fields.
  • TestLPAnalyticalBaseline (lp_cooptimize_test.py). The LP’s no-solar baseline case matches a closed-form calculation by hand, the simplest possible check that the optimizer isn’t just fitting noise.

Sources

  • Same capex sources as Claims 1 & 2. The methodological contribution here is the co-optimization LP itself (pipeline/steps/step9b_cooptimize_core.py). It jointly sizes PV, battery, and hourly dispatch under NEM 3.0’s actual rate structure, rather than a rule-of-thumb annual-match sizing heuristic.

Known limitations & open questions

  1. Non-bypassable charges (NBC) are assumed $0 for all utilities.

    Checked directly: at realistic NBC values (2–3¢/kWh), the billing formula is exactly mathematically invariant to NBC unless a month’s export credits fully offset the energy charge. This was verified not to happen for any county/month tested. Lower-risk than originally assumed, but not verified for every scenario.

  2. Retail rate and export-credit data have a known, checked staleness gap, worst for SDG&E and for export credits at all three utilities.

    Checked 2026-07-07, prompted by a direct question about whether current NEM rates were reflected:

    • PG&E retail rates: sourced from a PDF pulled March 9, 2026. Likely reflects PG&E’s March 2026 rate change (a 6.2% system-average decrease), but not independently re-verified against the live tariff.
    • SCE retail rates: sourced from screenshots taken March 4, 2026. Same caveat as PG&E.
    • SDG&E retail rates: no source document exists in the repository at all. Not stale, simply never sourced.
    • NEM 3.0 export credit (ACC) tables for all three utilities are dated 2024 (data/NEM3/*_2024_ACC_12x24_Export_Rates.xlsx). The 2026 export adder is publicly available (0.88¢/kWh standard, 3.6¢/kWh low-income) and hasn’t been checked against what the pipeline uses. This is the piece most likely to actually move Claim 1’s numbers, since export credit is central to whether a battery pencils out.
  3. The incentive-scenario comparison holds system size fixed.

    The LP sizes one physical system per county and scenario, then reports it under three incentive levels (full, half, no incentives). “No incentives” currently means “the bill impact of losing the rebate on the system you already built,” not “what you’d rationally build knowing there’d be no rebate.” A more behaviorally realistic design would re-solve the LP per incentive scenario. Documented as a real idea, not built. It would triple LP solves and change what the half and no-incentive columns mean.

  4. Claim 1’s statewide coverage is still 4 of 47 counties.

    Claims 2 and 3 are now fully statewide (47/47). Claim 1’s capex-threshold sweep is the one piece still limited to 4 counties. Scoped and timed today, deferred to a dedicated session.
